extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; scholars interested in ethics and metaphysics
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical treatment of punishment, eternal justice, and the meanings of 'good' and 'bad' within Schopenhauer's metaphysical framework. The text explains normative criteria for punishment (temporal vs eternal), the ethical efficacy of religious/mythical doctrines, and an account of virtue rooted in denial of the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of punishment: fulfilment of law as contract / deterrence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The immediate end of punishment is, in the particular case, the fulfilment of the law as a contract.” The one end of the law is deterrence: laws and punishment are essentially directed to the future, not the past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment must announce itself as inevitable in future cases so the law deters. Example cited: the old English indictment concluding that the convicted 'ought to be punished... to deter others from the like crimes in all time coming.' Ministers warn that unwarranted mercy may cause repetition of crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment must be based on positive law pre-established
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment is 'based upon the positive law alone, which before the offence has determined a punishment for it,' and this law is regarded as sanctioned by all members of the state (a common contract).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The threat of punishment functions as a counter-motive to outweigh motives for offence; effectiveness requires that the punishment be pre-established and actually carried out when offences occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment vs. revenge (temporal vs. mere requital)
rubrics_metrics.description: All requital of wrong by infliction of pain without any aim for the future is revenge and cannot be morally justified. Revenge is consolation for past suffering rather than a forward-directed social measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish punishment (future-oriented, law-fulfilment) from revenge (past-oriented, consolation). Anti-pattern: treating punishment as mere expiation or neutralisation without regard to deterrence—phrases like 'crime is expiated' are empty if they imply no future-directed social purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive-law punishment can legitimately treat the offender as a means (response to Kantian objection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant's maxim 'Man must always be treated as an end, never as a means' is criticized as vague; a punished criminal may be used 'merely as a means' (e.g. execution of a murderer) to restore public security in fulfilment of the state's contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification rests on the social contract: by enjoying security citizens have implicitly pledged life/freedom/property which can be forfeited. Thus lawful punishment that uses the offender instrumentally can be morally defensible within the contractual/deterrent framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eternal justice distinct from temporal justice; not a matter of delayed requital
rubrics_metrics.description: Eternal justice 'rules not the state but the world... is infallible, fixed, and sure.' The conception of requital implies time, therefore eternal justice cannot be mere requital; 'the punishment must here be so bound up with the offence that both are one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eternal justice is metaphysical and immediate: it cannot operate by postponement or by temporal balancing. This marks a different standard from legal/temporal justice and requires a different kind of apprehension of moral order.

rubrics_metrics.name: World-as-will framework: fate as indicator of moral worth
rubrics_metrics.description: The world is the objectivity of the one will to live; 'in all that [a being] experiences... it always gets its due.' Thus the general sadness and suffering of the world reflect the worth/guilt of beings as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer proposes using the overall fate and suffering distribution as a (metaphysical) standard for assessing moral worth: if beings as a whole were not, as a whole, worthless, their fate would not be so sad. This is a metaphysical criterion rather than an empirical legal one.

rubrics_metrics.name: To grasp eternal justice one must transcend the principium individuationis (see-through individuation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'principium individuationis' (veil of Mâyâ) causes individuals to see phenomena as separate; only by rising above knowledge bound to individuation and recognising the Ideas can one apprehend eternal justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, ordinary perception of separated individuals leads to puzzlement over apparent lack of retribution; true comprehension of justice requires the metaphysical insight that the inflicter and the sufferer share the same will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth of transmigration as an ethical instrument (practical substitute for philosophical truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The myth teaches that sufferings inflicted on others will be expiated in subsequent births (e.g., being reborn as brutes or lower castes), supporting conduct by aligning moral consequences with perceptible life examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not philosophically exact, the transmigration myth is an effective practical doctrine for guiding conduct among those who cannot attain metaphysical insight; it grounds ethical incentives in observable consequences and culturally salient images (rewards and punishments across rebirths).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'good' as conformity to a will's effort; good is essentially relative
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept 'good' 'signifies the conformity of an object to any definite effort of the will.' Everything that corresponds to a will's end is good—so 'good' is relative (e.g., good eating, good roads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish direct present satisfaction (agreeable) from indirect satisfaction with future reference (useful). Absolute or 'absolute good' is a contradiction under this account; ethical judgments are relative to will's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute good (summum bonum) construed as denial/self-effacement of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 'absolute good' is contradictory in the ordinary sense, metaphorically the 'complete self-effacement and denial of the will'—the true absence of will—alone silences its struggle and constitutes the summum bonum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a normative target: the radical negation of willing (ascetic/self-denying life) is the only genuine and lasting good; other measures are palliatives. This is both metaphysical and prescriptive for moral conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'bad' or 'evil' as persistent willingness to do wrong (denial of others' wills)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man always disposed to do wrong when opportunity offers, and without external restraint, is called 'bad'; such conduct 'denies the will which appears in other individuals' and seeks to destroy their existence or appropriate their powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This locates moral blame in egoism that elevates one's will at the expense of others. The ethical test for badness is whether one consistently acts to thwart or destroy the willing of other beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual sacrificial retribution as exemplary punishment (rare virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances where an individual stakes his life to murder an unpunishable oppressor and accepts execution are distinguished from ordinary revenge: such acts aim at an effect on the future (deterrence) and are not selfish, and thus resemble punishment done by private persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not state-administered and condemned by law, these rare acts have moral significance as attempts to serve eternal justice by example and to purify the Idea of man; they indicate a higher consciousness of unity of the will rather than mere consolation-seeking revenge.
